title: The Women of Weinsberg Carry Out Their Husbands
text:
In 1140 the German king Conrad III, of the Hohenstaufen family, was at war with the rival Welf dynasty. In December of that year he besieged the castle and town of Weinsberg, in Swabia, which was held for the Welfs. After the Welf relief army was defeated, the defenders had to surrender.

According to the Royal Chronicle of Cologne, written at the time, Conrad granted the women of the town permission to leave freely and to take with them whatever they could carry on their shoulders. The women came out through the gate carrying their husbands on their backs. The men had expected to be killed or imprisoned.

The later tellings add that Conrad's followers protested that this was not what the king had meant. Conrad is said to have answered that a king's word should not be twisted, and he let the men go. He was reportedly amused by the women's cleverness.

The ruined castle above Weinsberg has been known ever since as Weibertreu, "women's faithfulness." The story became a favorite in German literature, retold in a ballad by Gottfried August Burger, and the town still celebrates it.
lesson: Loyalty finds a way when the rules seem to leave none. Reading an offer carefully, and taking it at its word, can save what matters most.
people: Conrad III, the women of Weinsberg
source: Chronica regia Coloniensis (Royal Chronicle of Cologne), year 1140
caveat: The surrender is historical and the women's ruse is reported by a contemporary chronicle, but the dialogue and some details come from later retellings.
